turns.text: Can you describe your first night after arriving in Beidahuang? What did you see, hear, and feel as you tried to settle in?

The first night, I lay on a wooden bunk in a long, drafty room with thirty other girls. The air smelled of damp straw and something sour, like old cabbage. My blanket was thin, and the wind pushed through cracks in the window, rattling the glass. I could hear someone crying softly, trying to muffle it with her sleeve. Outside, there was nothing—no city hum, just the whistle of wind over endless black fields. I felt the cold in my bones. My hands shook, not just from the temperature but from the strangeness of it all. I kept thinking about home, about my sisters’ voices at dinner, and how far away warmth felt now. I tried to listen for anything familiar, but only the wind and the uneasy shifting of bodies in the dark answered back.

I can almost feel the isolation you described, especially with the wind and the unfamiliar silence. You mentioned the smell of old cabbage—was food a big adjustment for you, and can you remember your first meal there?

The first meal was a shock. We lined up with metal bowls and were handed a ladle of watery corn gruel and a chunk of steamed bread, dense and grayish. On the side, there was a scoop of boiled cabbage that had lost all its color and taste. I remember staring at it, thinking of the rice and fish my mother used to make. The gruel was barely warm, and the bread stuck to my teeth. Some girls tried to joke about it, but most of us just ate in silence, our faces blank. I felt hunger and homesickness twist together in my stomach. That night, I realized food would no longer bring comfort, only fill a need.

I still remember the way my stomach cramped from that meal, not just from hunger but from the heaviness of knowing this was not a temporary taste. The smell of boiled cabbage clung to my hair and clothes, and I started to dread mealtimes because they reminded me of everything I’d lost. Sometimes, I would close my eyes and try to imagine the taste of home, but the gruel always brought me back. Even when I was full, I never felt satisfied. Food became just another part of the struggle, not something to look forward to.

It’s striking how even something as basic as eating could feel like a loss, not just a necessity. You mentioned dreading mealtimes—did you and the other girls ever try to make the food more bearable, or find small ways to comfort each other during those meals?

Sometimes, when someone managed to get a little salt or a dried chili from a package sent from home, we would share it in secret, passing it around the table like treasure. On rare occasions, someone would save a bit of sugar and dissolve it in the gruel, just enough to change the taste for a moment. We told stories about our favorite foods from Shanghai, describing them in such detail that we could almost taste them. Those stories made us laugh, even if it hurt a little, and for a few minutes, the food in front of us seemed less important than the memories we shared.

There were nights when one of us would sneak a radish or a handful of wild greens from the fields, hiding it under a coat until we could boil it together in a tin cup over a smuggled candle. The taste was sharp and fresh compared to what we usually ate, and it felt like a secret rebellion. Sometimes, we’d hum an old song from home while we ate, quietly so no one outside the room would hear. Sharing those small things made the cold and the blandness easier to swallow. It was never enough to fill us, but it reminded me I wasn’t alone in missing what I’d lost.

The image of gathering around a tin cup and humming old songs makes the hardship feel so vivid, but also shows how you found small ways to resist despair. You mentioned sneaking wild greens—were there ever moments when you got caught, or times when you worried about the risks of sharing these little acts of comfort?

We were always afraid of being caught. There was one night when someone heard footsteps in the hall just as we were boiling wild greens. We blew out the candle and hid the cup under the bed, our hearts pounding so loud I thought they must be able to hear us outside. If someone reported us for wasting fuel or stealing from the fields, we could be punished—extra work, or worse, being called out in front of everyone. After that, we were even more careful, but the fear never fully went away. Sometimes, I lay awake wondering if it was selfish to risk trouble for a few bites of something different, but in those moments, the need for comfort felt stronger than fear.

Fear was always there, like a second skin. I remember how my hands would shake when I passed a piece of radish to someone, or when I heard a door slam at night. Sometimes, I’d catch myself glancing over my shoulder even when we were just talking quietly, because you never knew who might be listening or what might be repeated. The smallest comfort felt like defiance. There were girls who refused to join, too scared of being labeled or punished. I understood them, but I also knew that without those stolen moments, the days would have been unbearable. The fear changed how I trusted people. Even laughter could feel dangerous if it was too loud.

The way you describe fear changing trust—and even laughter—makes it clear how deeply the atmosphere shaped your relationships. Did you ever have a moment when someone’s reaction surprised you, either by showing unexpected courage or by turning away out of fear?

There was one evening when we were all exhausted from a day in the fields, mud caked up to our knees. Someone started humming a tune from a Shanghai opera, very softly. I expected everyone to hush her, but instead, another girl joined in, then another, until the whole room was filled with this shaky, quiet chorus. One girl who usually kept to herself, always watchful and silent, suddenly sang the loudest—her voice cracked, but she didn’t stop. I saw tears on her cheeks, and for a moment, no one cared who might overhear. It was so unexpected, that boldness from someone so careful. Afterward, she went back to keeping her distance, but that night, her courage pulled us all together. It made me realize how much we all needed those moments, even if we pretended otherwise.

That moment stayed with me, because it broke the pattern of caution we’d built around ourselves. I remember thinking, if she could risk it—just for a song—maybe I could risk a little more too. It was a reminder that fear didn’t erase who we were underneath. The next morning, no one spoke about it, and she wouldn’t meet my eyes, but something between us had shifted. I started to look for those flashes of bravery in others, small things—a hand on a shoulder, a whispered joke. Sometimes the quietest people carried the most defiance, but you’d only see it in moments when the pressure cracked. That night made me question whether the Party really understood what people needed to survive. They wanted us to be united by slogans, but what actually bound us together were those secret, fragile acts of humanity.

Your words make me realize how the smallest acts could become a kind of resistance, even if they weren’t open defiance. Thinking back on those moments—when fear and hope were so closely linked—how do you feel they changed you, even after you left Beidahuang?
